summary: Specifies extensions to the Teredo IPv6 transition protocol that add support for more types of NATs and more efficient communication.

eli5.summary: Teredo carries IPv6 over IPv4 through routers that rewrite addresses. These extras help it work with more kinds of such routers and run faster.

questions: does teredo work behind a symmetric nat
what is a teredo nonce trailer
subtitle: Six optional add-ons that let Teredo IPv6 tunneling work through more kinds of NATs and with less load on its servers.

tldr.problem: The original Teredo protocol gives up when a client sits behind a symmetric NAT, fails to connect many NAT pairs, and relies on Teredo servers to relay messages even for routine refreshes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6081 defines independent extensions (symmetric NAT support, UPnP, port preserving, sequential port prediction, hairpinning and server load reduction) plus a new TLV trailer format that carries nonces, ports and alternate addresses after the IPv6 packet.
tldr.outcome: More combinations of NATs can reach each other over Teredo, and combinations that still cannot connect fail within a finite time so the client can fall back to another address. The RFC updates RFC 4380.

today: RFC 6081 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 4380, the base Teredo specification. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC according to the metadata on this site.

sections.title: Why Teredo Needed Extensions
sections.content:
RFC 4380 defines Teredo, which lets a node behind one or more IPv4 NATs get IPv6 connectivity by tunneling packets over UDP. RFC 6081 adds extensions to it. They give Teredo support for more types of NATs and more efficient communication.

A Teredo client learns its mapped address/port (what the IPv4 Internet sees) from a Teredo server, and that mapping is embedded in its Teredo IPv6 address. A peer can then send IPv6 packets, encapsulated in IPv4 UDP, to that external address/port. Trouble starts when the NAT gives a different mapping to each peer.

The RFC also notes what happens when nothing works. If the qualification process fails, Teredo is not configured with an IPv6 address. For NAT combinations that no extension supports, the connectivity tests fail within a finite period, so the client can treat the destination as unreachable and try another address, such as a native IPv4 one.
sections.eli5: Some home routers hide your computer so well that friends cannot find it. These add-ons are extra tricks for finding each other anyway.

sections.title: NAT Types and Bubbles
sections.content:
The RFC leans on a vocabulary of NAT behaviors. A cone NAT maps all requests from one internal address/port to the same external address/port, and any external host can send back. A restricted NAT does the same mapping but only accepts packets from hosts the internal host has already sent to; address-restricted NATs check only the address, port-restricted NATs check address and port.

A symmetric NAT may map the same internal address/port to different external address/ports for different destinations. A port-symmetric NAT has one external IP address and varies only the port. A sequential port-symmetric NAT allocates external ports sequentially, with a delta typically 1 or 2. A port-preserving NAT keeps the mapped port equal to the local port when it can. Hairpinning lets a NAT route a packet from an internal host to another internal host through the NAT's own external address.

A Teredo bubble is a control message used to create a mapping in a NAT. A direct bubble goes straight to the peer's mapped address/port; an indirect bubble goes via the destination's Teredo server.
sections.eli5: A router can be like a doorman. Some let anyone in who knocks, some only let in people you already called, and some give you a new door number for every person you call. A bubble is a little knock that opens a door.

sections.title: Six Independent Extensions
sections.content:
The extensions are independent and can be implemented in isolation, with one exception: the UPnP-enabled Symmetric NAT Extension and the Port-Preserving Symmetric NAT Extension both require the Symmetric NAT Support Extension. An implementation can support any combination that respects that rule.

Figure 1 of the RFC is a matrix of source NAT type against destination NAT type. Each cell says whether the pair already works with RFC 4380 (Yes), works with the Symmetric NAT Support Extension (SNS), works with SNS plus UPnP, port-preserving or sequential port-symmetric support, or has no connectivity (No). For example, a symmetric-to-address-symmetric pair has no connectivity in any combination shown.

Sections 5.2 and 5.3 say implementations SHOULD support the Symmetric NAT Support and UPnP-enabled Symmetric NAT extensions. Both are optional.
sections.eli5: Think of six small tool add-ons for a Swiss army knife. You can pick any of them, but two of them only work if you also pick the first one.

sections.title: Symmetric NAT Support and Nonces
sections.content:
RFC 4380 suggests that a client that finds itself behind a symmetric NAT go offline, because a peer sees a different mapped address/port than the one embedded in the client's Teredo address, so incoming packets are dropped. With the Symmetric NAT Support Extension the client keeps using Teredo anyway.

If the peer is behind a cone or address-restricted NAT, communication can be set up either way. When the peer starts, it sends an indirect bubble through the client's server, the client answers with a direct bubble, and the peer remembers the mapped address/port from the direct bubble's IPv4/UDP headers. When the symmetric-NAT client starts, the peer's direct bubble would be dropped, so the peer instead responds with an indirect bubble through the client's server and the first case takes over.

To keep this safe, a client sending an indirect bubble MUST generate a random 4-byte value and put it in a Nonce Trailer, storing it as Nonce Sent. A direct bubble answering an indirect bubble MUST carry the same nonce. A received direct bubble MUST be accepted if its mapped address/port matches the one in the source Teredo address, or if it carries a nonce matching Nonce Sent. Otherwise it MUST be dropped.
sections.eli5: If you are behind a tricky router, a friend cannot guess your door number. So you both pass a secret word in your messages, and a visitor is let in if they say the right word.

sections.title: UPnP, Port Preserving and Port Prediction
sections.content:
Symmetric NAT support alone does not help when the peer is behind a port-restricted or symmetric NAT. Three further extensions attack that.

The UPnP-enabled Symmetric NAT Extension asks the NAT, before qualification, to reserve a mapping from the local address/port to a mapped address/port using the UPnP AddPortMapping function (description TEREDO, lease duration 0). The Teredo server then reflects that reserved mapping back, so it ends up in the Teredo IPv6 address, and the NAT forwards packets to it from any source. If AddPortMapping fails, the client continues without the extension.

The Port-Preserving Symmetric NAT Extension lets a client compare its mapped port with its local port during qualification; equal values mean the NAT is port-preserving. Such a client can listen on a randomly chosen local port, and if that port was not already used as a mapped port, the NAT reuses it. The random port is passed to the peer indirectly, via the servers.

The Sequential Port-Symmetric NAT Extension assumes, as a last resort, that a symmetric NAT which is not port-preserving is sequential. The client sends three packets: a router solicitation to the Teredo server address, a direct bubble to the peer, and a router solicitation to the secondary server address. It predicts the external port of the bubble to be midway between the ports seen for the two solicitations, then tells the peer. Other applications using the NAT in between can make the real port differ from the midpoint.
sections.eli5: One trick is to ask the router nicely to keep a door open for you. Another is to pick a door number first and hope the router keeps it. The last is guessing your next door number from the two numbers you got just before and after.

sections.title: Hairpinning and Server Load Reduction
sections.content:
Two clients behind the same NAT cannot reach each other if that NAT lacks hairpinning. The Hairpinning Extension fixes this: a client includes its local address/port in the indirect bubble it sends. The receiving client then sends direct bubbles both to the sender's mapped address/port and to the local address/port. If the NATs are in a multi-NAT hierarchy and the sender's NAT supports UPnP, the UPnP-mapped address/port can be included too. UPnP is only required when the clients are behind different NATs in such a hierarchy.

The Server Load Reduction Extension addresses refreshes. After a connection has been silent, NAT state between two peers should be refreshed, which normally needs an indirect bubble and so loads the Teredo server. With this extension the client sends a direct bubble that solicits a response, the peer answers with a direct bubble, and only if that fails does the client restart the full setup procedure from RFC 4380.

Section 5.1 also refines RFC 4380 on timers. The initial refresh interval parameter SHOULD be configurable and the default MUST be 30 seconds. An implementation MAY randomize the interval within an implementation-specific range, which MUST fall within 50% to 150% of the refresh interval.
sections.eli5: If two friends live in the same building but the doorman will not pass notes between them, they each knock on the inside door as well. To stay in touch, they ping each other directly instead of asking a helper every time.

sections.title: Trailers After the IPv6 Packet
sections.content:
The extensions use type-length-value trailers placed after the IPv6 packet inside the UDP payload. Each has a 1-byte Type, a 1-byte Length (the length of the Value in octets) and a variable Value. To make room for them, the RFC redefines "consistent" payload length: the IPv6 packet length (Payload Length plus the IPv6 header size) must be less than or equal to the UDP payload length.

The two highest-order bits of the Type say what to do with an unrecognized trailer: for 00, 10 and 11 skip it and continue; for 01 discard the packet. A client processes trailers in order and stops at the first malformed one, meaning less than 2 bytes remain, or fewer than 2 plus the Length value remain.

  • Nonce Trailer: Type 0x01, Length 0x04, a 4-byte nonce. It may appear in indirect and direct bubbles.
  • Alternate Address Trailer: Type 0x03. Only in indirect bubbles sent by a client. Length is 8, 14, 20 or 26 (2 reserved bytes plus 6 bytes per IPv4 address and port entry), and SHOULD be at most 14.
  • Neighbor Discovery Option Trailer: Type 0x04, Length 0x04, with DiscoveryType 0x00 (TeredoDiscoverySolicitation) or 0x01 (TeredoDiscoveryAdvertisement).
  • Random Port Trailer: carries the 2-byte external port the sender predicts its NAT has assigned. Section 4.5 gives its Type as 0x05, while the IANA table lists 0x02.
sections.eli5: Trailers are small sticky notes attached to the end of a letter. Each note says what kind it is and how long it is, so a reader who does not know a kind can skip it, unless the kind says to throw the whole letter away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations are the same as in Section 7 of RFC 4380, with two additions. The Hairpinning Extension could enable an amplification attack if a malicious user advertised a large number of port mappings in the Alternate Address Trailer, causing many direct bubbles in response. Section 4.3 therefore limits how many addresses a client accepts (a maximum of four).

The nonce prevents spoofed bubbles from directing traffic to the wrong place, so it must be random enough that attackers cannot predict it. The RFC points to RFC 4086 for randomness requirements. IANA created a new trailer Type registry, with new values assigned by Specification Required.
sections.eli5: Two safety rules: do not follow an endless list of addresses someone hands you, and make your secret word hard to guess.

items.title: Symmetric NAT Support
items.text: Keep using Teredo behind a symmetric NAT; nonces guard against spoofing.

items.title: UPnP-Enabled Symmetric NAT
items.text: Reserve a mapping via UPnP. Requires Symmetric NAT Support.

items.title: Port-Preserving Symmetric NAT
items.text: Use random local ports the NAT keeps. Requires Symmetric NAT Support.

items.title: Sequential Port-Symmetric NAT
items.text: Predict the external port from two router solicitations.

items.title: Hairpinning
items.text: Let clients behind the same NAT use local and alternate addresses.

items.title: Server Load Reduction
items.text: Refresh with direct bubbles that solicit a response.

messages.label: Direct bubble (dropped)
messages.note: Sent to the mapped address/port embedded in A's address, which A's NAT drops.

messages.label: Direct bubble
messages.note: B records the mapped address/port it came from.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the rest of the option; MUST be 0x04.

items.label: Nonce Trailer
items.desc: Authenticates a client behind a symmetric NAT.

items.label: Alternate Address Trailer
items.desc: Extra addresses for clients behind the same NAT; indirect bubbles only.

items.label: Neighbor Discovery Option Trailer
items.desc: Marks a direct bubble as soliciting or answering a response.

items.label: Random Port Trailer
items.desc: Predicted external port; Section 4.5 and the IANA table disagree on the Type.
